title: Advice to young players and his sons' music careers
summary: He talks about his twin sons, music education, and the shrinking work for jazz musicians.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: Advice to young musicians starting out

blocks.x: Okay, suppose I have a grandson and he’s a very good musician and he wants to be a jazz musician and he’s debating about college, or he just wants to go to New York City and be a musician, and I asked you — what do you think about that? Do you think I should encourage that kid to do such a thing?

Well along my lines were I wanted my — I had twin sons and I wanted one of them to be a piano player and the other one to be a drummer. Well the drummer became a very good drummer. I mean Grade 6 A solos in fifth or sixth grade. Then I had a set of vibes, because I figured if he’s going to get into percussion he’s got to learn all that. And then I had that bass in the corner. And one day he said, “what’s that?” I said, “it’s a string bass.” And he said — and I gave him his first bass lesson. Well that was it for him. I mean bass was his instrument. Now, he just took to it. I mean, it’s like me, piano, trumpet, drums, and then bass as a secondary instrument. He just loved it. And it hurt his hands. And his — my grandson — wanted to be like grandpa, play drums. That didn’t — I got a houseful of drums and he had drums at home. That didn’t work for him. Then he tried the bass, because of his father. That didn’t work. Now he’s got my father’s trumpet and he loves it. I mean he’s just playing in the band and everything else. But my son, who does play and makes a lot of money, I mean his pension’s ridiculous, is a professional musician at the Kennedy Center. His bass never even leaves the building. Although he did go with the National Symphony over to China and Korea and all this and that, touring, whenever they tour. But you’ve got to let them find their own way, man. It’s like you can’t say — first of all, the thing that amazes me is that they have all of these universities and schools now. I never attended an institution of higher learning. As I said, I didn’t go to Ithaca College so I never — but I gave seminars and clinics at colleges you know, when I was with those bands. They wanted to know what I knew, which I learned from the seat of my pants. But the thing is, the thing that I’m not getting is all of these schools have all of these things — all of this music that we didn’t have available to use, it’s all there now. I’ve got a whole big thing, stacks of music, which was not available when I was coming up. But a school teacher, he gets a job, he graduates from college, and I mean he might, if he’s lucky (and even that’s slowing down) get a cruise ship for a couple of months and get on one of those ships. But they’re even cutting back. A drummer might, because half of the music is a drummer playing along with a keyboard player and a soundtrack. So I mean all of that’s shutting down. The big bands are basically, I mean the Basie band, I mean how © Fillius Jazz Archive -29-

much can they work. Woody Herman’s band maybe works 15 weeks a year. There’s no bands to go on anymore. So going to New York, I mean even the studio work — now Broadway, I don’t know, because I never was into the Broadway — I worked at the Roseland Ballroom this and that. But I don’t see — it’s kind of like you go to college to learn how to be a teacher so you can teach somebody else how to be a teacher. But how do you get actually involved with what you’re being taught, other than to be a teacher. So it’s like there’s no light through the tunnel.
